The tank drum, also called the steel tongue drum, is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.241, a round steel slit-tongue drum. The usual construction turns an empty propane tank over and cuts away the bottom, then cuts seven to ten tongues radially in the base; an unused tank may also be used. The tongues can be tuned by the length of the cuts or by adding neodymium magnets, and can be set to a pentatonic scale, a diatonic scale, a chromatic scale or a chosen set of notes. The player strikes with the fingers or a mallet. Its predecessor, the wooden slit drum, was found in Africa, among the Aztecs, in Indonesia and in other civilisations, and was used for ritual and entertainment.
空靈鼓屬體鳴樂器，琴身與發聲體主要為鋼，常由丙烷氣瓶製成。製作者將氣瓶翻轉，切掉: The tank drum is an idiophone; its body and its sounding part are mainly steel, and it is often made from a propane cylinder. The maker turns the cylinder over, cuts or knocks out the bottom, and forms the tongues with radial cuts; the top of an unused cylinder can also be used. The tongues can be tuned by changing the length of the cuts or by gluing on weights, commonly neodymium magnets. Tuning may also grind away some metal, or add material by welding or fusing. The source does not state the materials of the other parts.
空靈鼓源自木製裂縫鼓。裂縫鼓曾由非洲、阿茲特克與印尼等多個古代文明獨立發展，用於: The tank drum comes from the wooden slit drum. Slit drums were developed independently by several ancient civilisations, in Africa, among the Aztecs, in Indonesia and elsewhere, and were used for ritual and entertainment. The modern steel tongue drum has several predecessors, the more important being Jim Doble's Whale Drum and Felle Vega's Tambiro, both from 1990. In February 2007 Dennis Havlena, inspired by the physical behaviour of the Tambiro and by the layout of the Hang's notes, made a round steel tongue drum with the tongues in a cross layout from an empty 20-pound propane tank; the name Hank Drum comes from Hang and tank. His design in turn inspired other steel tongue drums, and commercial versions are now made in many parts of the world.

鋼舌鼓音色溫潤悠揚，具有獨特的金屬質感。其聲音明亮而不刺耳，帶有柔和的泛音，彷彿: The steel tongue drum's timbre is warm and lingering, with a distinctive metallic quality. Its sound is bright without being harsh and carries soft overtones, as if an ethereal bell were mixed with the calm of a yoga singing bowl. Its range usually lies between the low middle and the middle register, its pitches are well defined, and striking different places can give as many as 8 to 15 pitches. It resonates as an idiophone: the whole steel sphere acts as the resonator, so the sound rings on naturally and fully. Beside the tank drum, a traditional marimba sounds drier, while the steel tongue drum has more depth and a meditative quality; beside a struck bell its timbre is softer and warmer, and better suited to a relaxed, healing musical atmosphere.
